html:
Surah Al-Kahf (The Cave) is the 18th surah of the Qur’an — one hundred and ten verses revealed in Makkah. Its name comes from the story of the Ashab al-Kahf (People of the Cave), the young believers in verses 9–26 who fled a tyrannical city, took shelter in a cave, and were preserved by Allah in a miraculous sleep for over three centuries. The surah weaves together four extended parables — the youths of the cave, the two garden owners (vv. 32–44), the meeting of Prophet Musa with al-Khidr (vv. 60–82), and Dhul-Qarnayn and the people behind the barrier (vv. 83–98) — each one testing a specific worldly trial: faith, wealth, knowledge, and power. Classical mufassirun from Ibn Kathīr onward read the surah as a complete manual for navigating the greatest of all trials, the arrival of the Dajjāl.

The protective virtue of Al-Kahf against the trial of the Dajjāl is firmly established in Sahih Muslim. The Prophet ☕ said: “Whoever memorises ten verses from the beginning of Surah al-Kahf will be protected from the Dajjāl.” This narration from Abū al-Darda’ is recorded in Sahih Muslim 809 — sahih by consensus, no scholar grades it below sahih. A parallel chain in the same collection (Muslim 809a) specifies the last ten verses, so acting on either end is proven Sunnah. The connection, as Ibn Kathīr explains, is thematic: the opening verses establish the Qur’an’s perfection and refute the attribution of a son to Allāh — a central Dajjālic lie — while the closing verses affirm that true success lies in sincere worship, not in the illusions the Dajjāl will offer.

The practice of reciting Al-Kahf on Friday rests on a well-attested but graded body of narrations. The strongest is from Abū Saʽīd al-Khudrī: “Whoever recites Surah al-Kahf on Friday, a light will shine for him between the two Fridays.” This appears in Sunan al-Dārimī 3407, Mishkāt al-Masābīḥ 2175, and al-Bayhaqī’s Sunan — graded hasan by al-Albānī and sahih in Sahih al-Jāmiʽ 6470. Ibn Ḥajar in Takhrīj al-Adhkār called it “the strongest report narrated concerning the virtue of reading Surah al-Kahf.” The Friday window, per the fiqh ruling preserved in IslamQA fatwa 10700, runs from Maghrib on Thursday to Maghrib on Friday, because the Islamic day begins at sunset. Weaker narrations about Friday recitation — the “light extending to Makkah” chains from Ibn Mardawayh, al-Ghazālī’s Iḥyā’ citations, and the forgiveness-until-the-next-Friday-plus-three-days wording — are daʽīf and should not be presented as the Prophet’s own words.

What makes Al-Kahf a weekly discipline rather than a magical charm is Ibn Kathīr’s observation that each of its four parables disarms one trial the Dajjāl will exploit. The youths of the cave resisted the trial of faith under state persecution. The garden owner was ruined by the trial of wealth. Mūsā learned patience under al-Khiḍr through the trial of knowledge — that one does not always know Allah’s hikmah behind events. Dhul-Qarnayn passed the trial of power by using his dominion to protect the weak, not to oppress them. Reciting the surah each Friday with reflection is a weekly rehearsal of the four responses the believer will need when the deception comes.
